title: Hooks — Automate Actions Around Claude's Work

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

By the end of this lesson you'll understand what hooks are, know five of Claude Code's core hook event types, and have a working hook that fires automatically when Claude Code modifies a file.

## What Are Hooks?

Hooks are shell commands that Claude Code runs automatically at specific points in its workflow — before Claude uses a tool, after it uses a tool, or when it finishes a response.

Think of hooks as automation triggers: *"every time Claude edits a file, also do X."* You define X, and Claude Code handles the triggering.

Hooks are defined in `.claude/settings.json` under the `hooks` key. This file lives in your project root (not inside the `commands/` folder).

Common real-world uses:
- **Auto-lint:** Run `prettier --write` or `eslint --fix` on every file Claude edits, so your code is always formatted
- **Auto-test:** Run your test suite after Claude makes changes, so you see immediately if something broke
- **Logging:** Write a log entry every time Claude modifies a file, so you have an audit trail
- **Notifications:** Send a desktop notification or beep when Claude finishes a long task
- **Git auto-commit:** Automatically create a commit after every accepted change

## Five Core Hook Event Types

Claude Code actually ships with a much longer list of hook events (SessionStart, Notification, UserPromptSubmit, and more). These five are the ones you'll use most often:

**`PreToolUse`**
Runs *before* Claude uses a tool. Use cases: confirm you're in the right directory, inject a reminder into Claude's context, log what Claude is about to do, block dangerous operations.

**`PostToolUse`**
Runs *after* Claude uses a tool. This is the most commonly used hook. Use cases: lint the file that was just edited, run tests after a code change, log what was modified, save context to memory files.

**`Stop`**
Runs when Claude finishes generating a complete response and is waiting for your input. Use cases: play a sound to signal Claude is done, send a desktop notification, summarize the session.

**`SubagentStop`**
Runs when a subagent (spawned by an orchestrator) finishes its work. Use cases: collect subagent outputs, trigger aggregation steps, log parallel agent results. Only relevant in multi-agent workflows (lesson 7-11).

**`PreCompact`**
Runs before Claude compresses a long conversation to free up context space. Use cases: save important context to a file before it gets compressed away, extract key decisions before the conversation summary replaces the full history.

Each hook type takes a list of matchers. The `matcher` field is a regex pattern that matches tool names — so you can trigger a hook only on `Write` calls, only on `Bash` calls, or any combination.

**User-level vs project-level hooks:** Hooks can live in two places:
- **Project-level:** `.claude/settings.json` in your project root — applies only to that project
- **User-level:** `~/.claude/settings.json` in your home directory — applies to ALL projects

User-level hooks are powerful for universal habits: a notification hook that always alerts you when Claude finishes, or a logging hook that always records AI actions to a central audit log. Project-level hooks are for project-specific rules: auto-running that project's test suite, enforcing that project's code style.

Both levels load simultaneously — user-level hooks AND project-level hooks both fire in a session.

**How your hook command receives data:** Claude Code does NOT pass tool details as separate environment variables. Instead, it writes a single JSON object to your hook command's **stdin**. Your script reads and parses that JSON. A typical payload looks like:

```json
{
  "session_id": "abc123",
  "cwd": "/current/working/directory",
  "hook_event_name": "PreToolUse",
  "tool_name": "Write",
  "tool_input": { "file_path": "src/app.js", "content": "..." }
}
```
For `PostToolUse`, the same JSON also includes a `tool_response` field with the tool's result.

| Field (in the stdin JSON) | Contains | Available in |
|----------|----------|-------------|
| `tool_name` | Name of the tool being used (e.g. `Write`, `Bash`) | PreToolUse, PostToolUse |
| `tool_input` | The arguments sent to the tool | PreToolUse, PostToolUse |
| `tool_response` | Result returned by the tool | PostToolUse only |
| `session_id` | Unique ID for this session | All types |

The one value that IS a real environment variable is **`CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR`** — the absolute path to your project root — available in every hook type. Use it to reference scripts stored in `.claude/hooks/` without hardcoding a path.

**Injecting feedback back to Claude:** If your hook exits with code `0`, Claude Code reads its stdout and includes it as context for its next action. This means a hook can actively inform Claude: write `echo 'WARNING: this function is deprecated'` and Claude will take that into account before proceeding.

**Matcher syntax:** The `matcher` field uses regular expressions. Common patterns:
- `"Write"` — fires only on Write tool calls (creating or overwriting files)
- `"Edit"` — fires only on Edit tool calls (in-place edits)
- `"Write|Edit"` — fires on either
- `"Bash"` — fires when Claude runs a shell command
- `".*"` — fires on every tool use (broad — use carefully)

## A Real-World Hooks Example

Here's a `settings.json` with three useful hooks for a web development project:

- A PostToolUse hook that logs which file was modified
- A Stop hook that prints a "Claude is done" message
- A PreToolUse hook that echoes a warning before any Bash command runs

**Hooks run with your user permissions.** A hook that runs `rm -rf` would actually delete files. Keep hooks simple and deterministic. If you're adding a hook that runs a linter or formatter, make sure that tool is installed and working before you wire it up — a failing hook will interrupt Claude's workflow.

sections.title: Set Up a File-Edit Hook
sections.content:
Add a PostToolUse hook that prints a message in the terminal every time Claude modifies a file. Verify it fires.

**Step 1 — Create or open `.claude/settings.json`:**
In VS Code Explorer, look for `.claude/settings.json` in your project root. If it doesn't exist, create it. (The `.claude/` folder should already exist from lesson 7-7 when you created the `commands/` subfolder.)

**Step 2 — Add the hook:**
Paste this content into `.claude/settings.json`:
```json
{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Write|Edit",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "echo Claude just edited a file"
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}
```
Save the file.

**Step 3 — Launch Claude Code:**
```
cd Documents\ai-course-projects
claude
```

**Step 4 — Trigger the hook:**
Ask Claude to make a small change to any file:
```
Add an HTML comment at the top of exercises/about-me.html that says
"Last updated by Claude Code"
```
Review the diff and accept it.

**Step 5 — Observe the hook output:**
After Claude applies the change, you should see:
```
Claude just edited a file
```
Printed in your terminal. That's your hook firing.

**Step 6 — Upgrade the hook (optional):**
Change the hook to something more informative. On Windows (PowerShell), update the command to:
```
echo File modified at %TIME%
```
This prints the time of each edit, giving you a lightweight audit log.

**Real-world extension:** If you have Prettier installed (`npm install -g prettier`), the file path isn't available as an environment variable — you need to read it from the JSON on stdin. Replace the `command` with a small PowerShell one-liner:
```powershell
powershell -Command "$j = [Console]::In.ReadToEnd() | ConvertFrom-Json; prettier --write $j.tool_input.file_path"
```
This auto-formats every file Claude touches. That single hook eliminates an entire class of manual formatting work.

sections.question: You add a PostToolUse hook that runs tests after every file edit. Claude Code edits 10 files in sequence. What is the potential problem?
options: The hook will not run after multiple edits
Tests run after every single edit, even when the project is in a broken intermediate state — causing many test failures for temporarily incomplete code
The hook will slow down Claude Code permanently
Tests cannot be run from hooks
sections.explanation: Running tests after every individual edit causes "intermediate state" failures — when implementing a feature that requires changes to multiple files, the project is broken between edits. A smarter approach: run tests only after Claude Code indicates it's done with a task, or add a delay. Use the `Stop` hook (runs when the session ends) instead of `PostToolUse`, or add a hook that only runs tests if the preceding edit was the last in a sequence.

sections.question: A PreToolUse hook exits with code 1 when a dangerous command is detected. What happens to Claude Code?
options: Claude Code ignores the hook and runs the command anyway
The tool call proceeds anyway — exit code 1 is treated as a non-blocking error in Claude Code; only exit code 2 actually blocks the tool use
Claude Code crashes and loses all progress
Exit code 1 blocks the action, same as exit code 2
sections.explanation: This is the most common mistake when writing Claude Code hooks. Exit code 1 (or any non-zero code other than 2) is a *non-blocking* error — Claude Code shows an error notice in the transcript, but the tool call proceeds anyway. Only **exit code 2** is the designated blocking signal: Claude Code reads the hook's stderr as the reason and does not proceed with the tool use. Any PreToolUse hook meant to actually enforce a rule must exit with code 2, not 1.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 7-8.** You've configured a working hook, understand five of Claude Code's core hook event types, and know that hooks receive their data as JSON on stdin (not environment variables) and only block a tool call when a hook exits with code 2. Hooks are one of Claude Code's most powerful features for building reliable, repeatable workflows. Next: the memory system.
